hook: The first global commodity wasn't oil. It was sugar.
b1Text: England's King Henry III was ready to pay roughly US$450 in today's money for three pounds of sugar.
b2Text: Sugar travelled with a second 'commodity': enslaved Africans, sold in the Caribbean and the Americas.
b3Text: Plantations grew, crushed and boiled the cane on one site, using enslaved labour at every step.
b4Text: Investments in the sugar colonies were four to seven times more profitable than investments in England.
b5Text: By 1774, raw sugar made up one-fifth of all British imports, more than any other good.

hook: The slave plantation wasn't invented in the Americas.
b1Text: The Black Death drastically reduced the peasant labour supply around the Mediterranean.
b2Text: Island rulers imported enslaved people from North Africa to work the sugar.
b3Text: Merchant families invested in these plantations: the marriage of merchant capital and modern slavery.
b4Text: Land from the Portuguese king, capital from Venice or Genoa, enslaved people from Africa.
b5Text: Portugal carried the São Tomé model to Brazil. From there it spread to the Caribbean and North America.

hook: Planters found it cheaper to replace people than to keep them alive.
b1Text: Planting holes each first-gang worker had to dig by hand, every day.
b2Text: Harvest-season shifts in the mills and boiling houses, six days a week.
b3Text: A Barbados planter estimated a sugar estate would kill all 100 of its enslaved workers in 19 years.
b4Text: Newly arrived enslaved people who died within their first year, by one contemporary estimate.
b5Text: Owners tracked return on investment like spreadsheets. Time-and-motion studies came before Taylorism.

hook: At least ten million people landed. The real number seized was far higher.
b1Text: Enslaved Africans estimated to have landed in the Americas and the Caribbean.
b2Text: Plausible total seized, counting deaths during capture, marches, detention and the Middle Passage.
b3Text: Africans forced onto British ships, 1640–1807. About 2.7 million survived the crossing.
b4Text: Muskets exchanged for one enslaved person: early 1700s versus the end of that century.
b5Text: Population growth in Asia and Europe, 1600s–1800s. Africa's stayed almost flat, and fell in many regions.

hook: Before the textile mills, some of Britain's earliest factories refined slave-grown sugar.
b1Text: Refineries from Plymouth to Glasgow: coal, heat, specialised equipment and disciplined labour.
b2Text: Growth of British sugar imports from 1700 to 1800: about 21,845 to 152,407 tonnes.
b3Text: Share of Jamaica's sugar exports shipped to Britain between 1682 and 1701.
b4Text: Share of capital for Britain's expansion in 1770 that came from slave-trade profits (Engerman).
b5Text: Extra tariff Britain put on Indian sugar to protect its refiners and Caribbean plantations.

hook: The global financial system grew out of sugar, silver and slavery.
b1Text: Spain issues the first asiento: a licence to sell enslaved Africans to its colonies.
b2Text: Share of the world's silver from Spanish America, 1494–1850, mined in Potosí and Mexico.
b3Text: The Spanish silver dollar was accepted for trade across Asia, the Americas and much of Europe.
b4Text: Control of sugar and the trade in enslaved people helped make each the reserve currency of its era.
b5Text: Modern capitalism's configuration of power dates back at least around 500 years.
